conventions.convention: Coordinates have fixed order 1,…,n, with n≥1. L and U are the negatives of the strict lower and upper parts, so A=D−L−U; for Hermitian A, U=L*.

Richardson takes a real relaxation parameter, rejects ω=0, and performs exactly the requested nonnegative iteration budget after validation. A completed finite budget supplies no convergence or accuracy certificate.
Jacobi updates all coordinates simultaneously from the previous iterate; a zero diagonal entry causes pivot-failure at the least such index.
Gauss–Seidel uses forward substitution in increasing coordinate order, using new lower-index coordinates and old upper-index coordinates.

SOR is operationally defined for every real ω≠0 when all diagonal pivots are nonzero. Its splitting is Mω=ω⁻¹D−L and Nω=(ω⁻¹−1)D+U; the interval (0,2) is a convergence condition, not an input restriction.
Strong connectivity uses directed positive-entry edges and allows paths of length zero, including the singleton graph.

The SOR equivalence assumes n≥1, Hermitian A with strictly positive diagonal, and real ω≠0. Convergence means exact-arithmetic convergence to the unique solution for every right-hand side and every initial vector.

load_bearing.statement: For A over R or C with n≥1 and fixed coordinate order, D is its diagonal and L,U are its negative strict lower and upper parts. Thus A=D−L−U; if A=A*, then U=L*.

For a nonnegative real n×n matrix C, n≥1, with row sums at most 1, strongly connected positive-entry graph, and at least one strict row, Cⁿ1<1 coordinatewise, and v=Σₖ₌₀∞Cᵏ1 converges coordinatewise with v>0 and Cv<v.
After dimension and nonzero-diagonal checks, perform m simultaneous updates D x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(L+U)x⁽ᵏ⁾+b and return completed with x⁽ᵐ⁾; m may be zero.
After dimension and nonzero-diagonal checks, perform m increasing-order forward solves (D−L)x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=Ux⁽ᵏ⁾+b and return completed with x⁽ᵐ⁾; m may be zero.
After dimension, real ω≠0, and nonzero-diagonal checks, use Mω=ω⁻¹D−L and Nω=(ω⁻¹−1)D+U, perform m forward solves Mωx⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=Nωx⁽ᵏ⁾+b, and return completed with x⁽ᵐ⁾.
For n≥1 and real A satisfying |aᵢᵢ|>Σⱼ≠ᵢ|aᵢⱼ| in every row, Jacobi and fixed-order Gauss–Seidel converge in exact arithmetic to the unique solution of Ax=b for every real b and initial vector.

For n≥1, Hermitian complex A with strictly positive diagonal, and real ω≠0, SOR converges to the unique solution of Ax=b for every complex b and initial vector if and only if A is positive definite and 0<ω<2.

concerns.concern: Proof step 2.2 introduces an arbitrary initial error, and step 3.1 then asserts “Moreover δ₀≠0” from invertibility of A. This needs the restriction e⁽⁰⁾≠0, stated only in the final conclusion of step 3.1: for e⁽⁰⁾=0, δ₀=0. Fixing an arbitrary nonzero initial error before this assertion closes the proof immediately; the theorem itself remains supported.
